newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Sammi troubles spark worries over tightening credit.
newsitem.headline: Sammi troubles spark worries over tightening credit.

text.p: Fears of tightening credit in the wake of South Korea's second major corporate crisis this year sent South Korean interest rates to a new 18-month high and pushed the won lower, analysts said on Wednesday.
Sammi Steel Co sought protection from its creditors on Tuesday along with four other affiliates of the Sammi Group, one of the nation's top 30 conglomerates.
It was the second steel maker to hit the rocks this year, following Hanbo Steel Co, which foundered in January.

"Despite the fact that the Bank of Korea remains flexible in supplying money into the system....most of that money is sitting in financial institutions and not going to the corporations," said Lim Chun-soo, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets in Seoul.
Yields on benchmark three-year corporate bonds closed at 12.85 percent, up from Tuesday's 12.75 percent.
Brokers said liquidity showed signs of drying up after news of Sammi's difficulties.
"The news chilled sentiment," said a Samsung Securities broker.
But another dealer said there was market talk the central bank would loosen its purse strings to avoid a chain reaction of failures, as it had done after Hanbo's collapse.
"In the wake of Sammi's failure, there are rumours the Bank of Korea is changing its previous stance of tightening short term money supply," said a Korea Development Bank dealer.
A central Bank of Korea official, who declined to be identified, said the central bank was carefully watching the current situation but as of Wednesday had no plans to supply additional funds.
"Liquidity isn't tight at the moment," he said. "But banks are nervous about the current situation and they are worried there will be a fund shortage."
Foreign exchange dealers said players were concerned the latest corporate crisis would reduce further foreign lending and squeeze the supply of dollars.
As a result of the Hanbo failure, which exposed weak credit analysis and corrupt lending practices, South Korean banks are paying more for overseas loans.
Three top bankers are now on trial for bribery in a loans scandal linked to the collapse.
The won continued its slide against the U.S. unit, closing at a low of 884.80, compared to Tuesday's close of 883.10.
The won has lost 3.9 percent of its value against the dollar this year.
"Sammi is definitely one of the factors behind the won's weakness," said a European bank dealer.

Other factors pressuring the local currency are the nation's mounting trade deficit, the dollar's strength against the Japanese yen on world markets, and foreigners pulling out of the local stock market.

Extra demand for dollars is also coming from commercial banks facing difficulties borrowing from Japanese counterparts, which are tightening credit lines before the end of the financial year ending in March. (Conversion $1 = 882.60)
